```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5)
options(mdir.quiet = TRUE)
```

A view whose columns are ordered measurements, such as a time course, can be
modelled with `type = "GP"` instead of a multivariate normal. Each cluster then
has a mean *curve*, a Gaussian process over the measurement index with a squared
exponential kernel, so neighbouring measurements are tied together and the
cluster is described by three hyperparameters (amplitude, length scale and noise)
instead of a full covariance matrix. This vignette fits one such view alongside an
ordinary view, and shows how the sampler's one tuning setting, the proposal
windows of those hyperparameters, behaves. `"TAGPM"` adds an outlier component to
the same model. The workflow of the other steps (priors, convergence, predictive
checks) is in the `mdir-workflow` vignette.

## Data

Two groups of items with different smooth curves over eight time points, and a
second view on which the same groups differ.

```{r data}
library(mdir)
set.seed(2)

N <- 40
P <- 8
time <- seq_len(P)
truth <- rep(1:2, each = N / 2)
curves <- rbind(2 * sin(time / 2), -1.5 * cos(time / 3) + 1)

X_time <- curves[truth, ] + matrix(rnorm(N * P, sd = 0.5), N, P)
X_other <- matrix(rnorm(N * 2, mean = ifelse(truth == 1, 0, 3)), N, 2)
rownames(X_time) <- rownames(X_other) <- seq_len(N)
X <- list(X_time, X_other)
types <- c("GP", "MVN")
K_max <- c(4, 4)
```

The columns are taken to be one unit apart, so the length scale is in units of the
spacing between measurements. `densityPrior()` holds the priors on the
hyperparameters, which are documented in `?densityPrior`: the length scale is kept
above `gp_min_length` (one spacing by default), since a shorter one cannot be
distinguished from measurement noise, and the amplitude and noise are partially
pooled across clusters.

## Fitting, and the proposal windows

The amplitude, length scale and noise of each cluster have no closed-form
conditional, so they are updated by Metropolis-Hastings random walks on the log
scale. Their step sizes (`proposal_windows`) are the one place where the sampler
needs a user-chosen scale. By default `mdir` adapts them during the first half of
the run towards an acceptance rate of about 0.44, the rate that is near optimal for
a one-dimensional random walk (Gelman, Roberts and Gilks, 1996), with a
Robbins-Monro recursion whose steps decay (Garthwaite, Fan and Sisson, 2016), and
then fixes them, so the retained draws come from a chain with fixed
proposals. The settings live in `mdirControl()`:

```{r control}
mdirControl()
```

```{r fit}
fit <- fitMDI(X, n_chains = 3, n_iter = 20000, thin = 10, types = types,
              K_max = K_max, convergence_burn = 10000, verbose = FALSE,
              control = mdirControl(n_burn = 10000))
fit
```

The adapted windows are returned with each chain, a vector of
(amplitude, length, noise) per view; one column per chain below, for view 1:

```{r windows}
sapply(fit, function(chain) chain$final_proposal_windows[[1]])
```

To see what the adaptation does, start the windows too small and too large, and
compare the acceptance rate of the updates with and without it. A rate far from
0.44 is not an error, but it makes the chain mix slowly: tiny steps accept nearly
always and move very little, and huge ones are nearly always rejected.

```{r adaptation}
acceptance <- function(chain) {
  ac <- chain$acceptance_count[[1]]
  K <- length(ac) / 3
  # an empty cluster makes no proposals and shows a rate of 0
  vapply(0:2, function(h) mean(ac[h * K + seq_len(K)][ac[h * K + seq_len(K)] > 0]), numeric(1))
}
run <- function(window, auto_tune) {
  chain <- callMDI(X, n_iter = 4000, thin = 5, types = types, K_max = K_max,
                   check_prior = FALSE,
                   control = mdirControl(proposal_windows = list(rep(window, 3), NULL),
                                         auto_tune = auto_tune, n_burn = 10000))
  c(start_window = window, auto_tune = auto_tune,
    setNames(round(acceptance(chain), 2), c("amplitude", "length", "noise")))
}
as.data.frame(rbind(run(0.002, FALSE), run(0.002, TRUE), run(8, FALSE), run(8, TRUE)))
```

(The rates with `auto_tune = TRUE` are averages over the whole run, so they include
the adaptation period.) Only the windows of the Gaussian process hyperparameters are
adapted. The random walk on the log of the mass parameter (standard deviation 0.3)
and the one on the spread of the population of amplitudes and noises (0.5) have
fixed scales; whether they should be tuned too is open.

## Convergence

The convergence report concerns quantities that do not depend on how the clusters
are labelled. The hyperparameters themselves are per cluster, and cluster 1 of one
chain is not cluster 1 of another, so they are not compared across chains;
`as_draws()` keeps the pooled
hyperparameters (`pooled[v,j]`, the parameters of the populations of amplitudes and
noises shared by the clusters of view `v`; `?as_draws.mdir_fit`), which are label
free.

The chains here are short, and the report above still flags the mass parameters
(`Rhat` about 1.06); run longer chains before reporting anything.

```{r draws, eval = requireNamespace("posterior", quietly = TRUE)}
draws <- posterior::as_draws(fit, burn = 10000)
posterior::summarise_draws(draws, "mean", "rhat", "ess_bulk")
```

## What the fit finds

```{r partition}
pooled <- predictFromMultipleChains(fit, burn = 10000)
table(fitted = pooled$pred[[1]], truth = truth)
```

The posterior mean hyperparameters of each cluster that is occupied in view 1, in
one chain after burn in. The clusters are labelled arbitrarily, so this describes
this chain only. The length scale is in units of the spacing between measurements.

```{r hypers}
chain <- fit[[1]]
hypers <- chain$hypers[[1]]
keep <- seq(floor(dim(chain$N_k)[3] / 2) + 1, dim(chain$N_k)[3])
occupied <- which(rowMeans(chain$N_k[, 1, keep]) > 1)
round(data.frame(
  cluster = occupied,
  mean_size = rowMeans(chain$N_k[occupied, 1, keep]),
  amplitude = colMeans(hypers$amplitude[keep, occupied, drop = FALSE]),
  length = colMeans(hypers$length[keep, occupied, drop = FALSE]),
  noise = colMeans(hypers$noise[keep, occupied, drop = FALSE])
), 2)
```

The two clusters of about 20 items are the two groups, and their noise estimates
(about 0.26 and 0.31) are close to the true variance 0.25. The other cluster is
occupied by one item on average, so its hyperparameters are mostly the prior.

## Unequally spaced measurements

By default the columns are one unit apart. If they are not, say so with
`time_points`, a list with an entry for each view (`NULL` for the views that are not
Gaussian processes) giving the position of each column. The positions need not be
equally spaced, and the length scales are then in their units. The positions are
the same for every item: if items were measured at different times, make each time
a column and leave the cells of the unmeasured items as `NA`, which the sampler
imputes. The fit is less informative about the curve where many items are missing,
but the cluster curves are still recovered if enough items are observed at each
position, as here, where 30% of the cells are missing.

```{r irregular}
set.seed(31)
times <- c(0, 0.4, 1.5, 2, 3.7, 5, 5.3, 8, 9.5, 12)
group_curves <- rbind(2 * sin(times / 2.5), -1.5 * cos(times / 4) + 1)
Y <- group_curves[truth, ] + matrix(rnorm(N * length(times), sd = 0.4), N)
rownames(Y) <- seq_len(N)
Y[sample(length(Y), 0.3 * length(Y))] <- NA

irregular <- callMDI(list(Y), n_iter = 6000, thin = 5, types = "GP", K_max = 3,
                     time_points = list(times), control = mdirControl(n_burn = 3000))
keep <- 601:1201
sizes <- rowMeans(irregular$N_k[, 1, keep])
big <- order(sizes, decreasing = TRUE)[1:2]
P_t <- length(times)
est <- sapply(big, function(k) colMeans(irregular$parameters[[1]][keep, (k - 1) * P_t + seq_len(P_t)]))
matplot(times, est, type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 1, col = c("black", "grey50"),
        xlab = "time", ylab = "posterior mean curve")
matlines(times, t(group_curves), lty = 2, col = c("black", "grey50"))
legend("topright", c("estimate", "truth"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

The floor on the length scale (`gp_min_length` in `densityPrior()`) is a multiple of
the smallest spacing between positions, here 0.3. A very close pair of positions
therefore lowers the floor for all the others; raise `gp_min_length` if that lets
the length scale fall below what the rest of the measurements can resolve.

## Checking the fit

```{r posterior-predictive}
post_sims <- simulatePosteriorPredictive(fit, X, n_draws = 50, burn = 10000)
plotPredictiveCheck(X, post_sims, view = 1, column = 1)
```

## References

Garthwaite, P. H., Fan, Y. and Sisson, S. A. (2016). Adaptive optimal scaling of
Metropolis-Hastings algorithms using the Robbins-Monro process. *Communications in
Statistics - Theory and Methods*, 45(17), 5098-5111.

Gelman, A., Roberts, G. O. and Gilks, W. R. (1996). Efficient Metropolis jumping
rules. In *Bayesian Statistics 5*, 599-607. Oxford University Press.
